title: The Question Comes First
thesis: UAA’s new EEG adds the ability to collect brain signals around tasks its researchers choose, alongside the public datasets they already use.
valence: Celebratory, curious and warm about acquired student research capability
supporting_facts: UAA announced a DSI-24 acquisition for its AI and Robotics Lab on September 9th and documented training.
Egorov describes using public EEG datasets and anticipating collection for his own tasks.
Reading and programming studies are planned, so the instrument creates a research option rather than a reported result.
counterpoint: Public datasets already enable useful research. Owning hardware neither makes existing data obsolete nor establishes a correct interpretation.
falsifying_observation: If the lab could not collect usable signals around its chosen tasks, the claimed addition to experimental choice would not hold.
second_movement: Move from choosing a task to testing what the resulting signal can support. If an eventual model claims to work for new people, its test needs people absent from training. This is editorial methods context, never an allegation about UAA.

runner_up_angles.angle: New-person performance as the central thesis
runner_up_angles.reason_lost: The source announces equipment and planned studies, not a cross-person model claim. Conditional methods test belongs in Act3.

runner_up_angles.angle: New local findings must be impossible with public data
runner_up_angles.reason_lost: Unsupported comparative requirement. Existing public data remains valuable.

synthesis: Use experimental choice as the main claim, honest source boundaries from angle1, conditional held-out-person test from angle3.
